confidence_note: Strong evidence across lexical, thematic, and structural criteria; multiple scholars have noted the concentric shape of Ruth 1, with the central unit (Orpah's departure and Ruth's clinging) carrying decisive theological weight. The inclusio of Bethlehem and the inversion of 'going out full/returning empty' provide firm outer brackets.

elements.label: A
elements.summary: A man of Bethlehem-Judah goes to sojourn in Moab with his wife and two sons during a famine.
elements.text_excerpt: וַיֵּלֶךְ אִישׁ מִבֵּית לֶחֶם יְהוּדָה לָגוּר בִּשְׂדֵי מוֹאָב ('a man went from Bethlehem-Judah to sojourn in the fields of Moab')

elements.label: B
elements.summary: Death of Elimelech and both sons leaves Naomi bereft of husband and children in a foreign land.
elements.text_excerpt: וַתִּשָּׁאֵר הָאִשָּׁה מִשְּׁנֵי יְלָדֶיהָ וּמֵאִישָׁהּ ('the woman was left without her two children and her husband')

elements.label: C
elements.summary: Naomi hears that the LORD has visited his people with food and sets out to return to Judah with her daughters-in-law.
elements.text_excerpt: כִּי פָקַד יְהוָה אֶת עַמּוֹ לָתֵת לָהֶם לָחֶם ('that the LORD had visited his people to give them bread')

elements.label: D
elements.summary: Naomi urges both daughters-in-law to return to their mothers' houses; both weep and insist on going with her.
elements.text_excerpt: שֹׁבְנָה אִשָּׁה לְבֵית אִמָּהּ ('return, each to her mother's house') / וַתִּבְכֶּינָה ('and they wept')

elements.label: X
elements.summary: Naomi's anguished speech: she has no more sons to give, and the hand of the LORD has gone out against her — the theological crux of bitterness and divine absence.
elements.text_excerpt: כִּי יָצְאָה בִי יַד יְהוָה ('for the hand of the LORD has gone out against me')

elements.label: D'
elements.summary: Orpah kisses Naomi and returns, but Ruth clings — the decisive moment of loyalty contrasting with the earlier insistence of both women.
elements.text_excerpt: וַתִּשַּׁק עָרְפָּה לַחֲמוֹתָהּ וְרוּת דָּבְקָה בָּהּ ('Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her')

elements.label: C'
elements.summary: Ruth's declaration of loyalty: she will go where Naomi goes, her people will be Naomi's people, and the LORD will be her God — a reversal of the earlier departure motif.
elements.text_excerpt: עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָי ('your people shall be my people and your God my God')

elements.label: B'
elements.summary: Naomi ceases urging Ruth, and they travel together until they arrive in Bethlehem — reversal of the isolation motif.
elements.text_excerpt: וַתֵּלַכְנָה שְׁתֵּיהֶם עַד בֹּאָנָה בֵּית לָחֶם ('so the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem')

elements.label: A'
elements.summary: Naomi returns to Bethlehem-Judah; she declares she went out full and returns empty, yet the LORD has afflicted her — closure of the geographical and theological frame.
elements.text_excerpt: אֲנִי מְלֵאָה הָלַכְתִּי וְרֵיקָם הֱשִׁיבַנִי יְהוָה ('I went out full but the LORD has brought me back empty')

pivot.label: X
pivot.summary: Naomi's speech to her daughters-in-law is the structural center, explicitly naming the LORD's hand turned against her and eliminating any hope of levirate redemption through her womb — the nadir of the entire book.
pivot.theological_weight: At the exact center stands Naomi's confession that YHWH himself has become her adversary (יָצְאָה בִי יַד יְהוָה), inverting the exodus-blessing theology and framing the human loyalty about to be displayed by Ruth as a divine response to abandonment. This lament is the theological problem the rest of the book must resolve: can hesed from a foreign woman reverse what divine affliction has initiated?

correspondences.evidence: Both units share בֵּית לֶחֶם יְהוּדָה as the geographical anchor; A opens with a man going out (וַיֵּלֶךְ), while A' closes with Naomi's confession that she went out full (מְלֵאָה הָלַכְתִּי) and returns empty — lexical and thematic inversion of the root הלך and the motif of fullness/emptiness.

B describes Naomi left alone (וַתִּשָּׁאֵר) after the death of husband and sons; B' shows Naomi no longer alone as the two women walk together (שְׁתֵּיהֶם) to Bethlehem — the root שׁאר (remnant/left) and the contrast between solitary bereftness and restored companionship.

C introduces YHWH's visitation of his people with לֶחֶם (bread/food), motivating the return journey; C' presents Ruth's solemn oath invoking YHWH (וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָי) and sealing the return — both units pivot on YHWH's identity and the motivation for going back to the land.

D shows both women weeping and insisting they will go with Naomi (שׁוּב repeated as imperative to return); D' shows the split — Orpah returns (וַתָּשָׁב) while Ruth refuses, the root שׁוּב appearing emphatically in both units to mark diverging responses to the same call.

methodology_citations: Dorsey (1999), pp. 15-17 on concentric patterning in Hebrew narrative prose; pp. 133-134 on the book of Ruth; Walsh (2001), pp. 8-14 on lexical and thematic correspondences as structural indicators; Lund (1942), pp. 40-41 on the law of the shift at the center and the theological primacy of the pivot.
theological_significance: The concentric structure reveals that the entire first chapter is organized around Naomi's bitter lament about divine affliction (vv. 11-13), making her theology — not Ruth's loyalty — the framing problem of the story. The symmetrical arrangement demonstrates that Ruth's famous confession (C') is the literary and theological answer to the LORD's visitation for bread (C), suggesting that Ruth's hesed is itself an enacted form of divine provision. The structure thus argues that human loyalty and divine action are not in tension but are concentric realities, with the bitterest moment at the center surrounded by ever-widening circles of returning, belonging, and arrival.
scholarly_citations: Dorsey (1999, p. 134) outlines a concentric structure for Ruth 1 centered on the two women's response to Naomi's entreaty. Katharine Sakenfeld ('Ruth,' Interpretation, 1999, pp. 24-29) notes the theological irony of the central lament and its function as the problem the narrative resolves; Phyllis Trible (God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality, 1978, pp. 168-172) identifies the formal and thematic framing of the chapter around Naomi's bitterness and Bethlehem as inclusio markers.

bibcrit_hypothesis.title: Ruth 1 as Theological Complaint Framed by Hesed
bibcrit_hypothesis.reasoning: The concentric shape of Ruth 1 suggests a single compositional hand who deliberately placed Naomi's lament at the center and constructed mirror panels of departure and arrival, weeping and clinging, around it. This design is inconsistent with source-critical fragmentation and supports the unity of the chapter as a carefully crafted theological overture to the book as a whole. The pivot's identification of YHWH as the source of affliction creates a deliberate narrative tension that the concentric structure itself promises will be resolved — indicating that the author understood literary architecture as a theological argument.
